entries.ad103b34e5ce2fe70e940c45b4f5e471c9b94d3f: <div sID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="23" osisID="Job.23" sID="Job.23"/> <div eID="gen9807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9808" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins Job's reply to Eliphaz. In this reply he takes no notice of his friends, either because he saw it was to no purpose or because he liked the good counsel Eliphaz gave him in the close of his discourse so well that he would make no answer to the peevish reflections he began with; but he appeals to God, begs to have his cause heard, and doubts not but to make it good, having the testimony of his own conscience concerning his integrity. Here seems to be a struggle between flesh and spirit, fear and faith, throughout this chapter. I. He complains of his calamitous condition, and especially of God's withdrawings from him, so that he could not get his appeal heard (<reference osisRef="Job.23.2-Job.23.5">ver. 2-5</reference>), nor discern the meaning of God's dealings with him (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), nor gain any hope of relief, <reference osisRef="Job.23.13-Job.23.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. This made deep impressions of trouble and terror upon him, <reference osisRef="Job.23.15-Job.23.17">ver. 15-17</reference>. But, II. In the midst of these complaints he comforts himself with the assurance of God's clemency (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6-Job.23.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>), and his own integrity, which God himself was a witness to, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10-Job.23.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. Thus was the light of his day like that spoken of, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.6-Zech.14.7">Zech. xiv. 6, 7</reference>, neither perfectly clear nor perfectly dark, but "at evening time it was light."
entries.12517d80b2b27130eaba9cd217f642e4a276f808: <div eID="gen9809" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9808" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Reply of Job to Eliphaz; Job Appeals from Man to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Job answered and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> Even to day <hi type="italic">is</hi> my complaint bitter: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. <hi type="super">3</hi> Oh that I knew where I might find him! <hi type="italic">that</hi> I might come <hi type="italic">even</hi> to his seat! <hi type="super">4</hi> I would order <hi type="italic">my</hi> cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. 5 I would know the words <hi type="italic">which</hi> he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me. <hi type="super">6</hi> Will he plead against me with <hi type="italic">his</hi> great power? No; but he would put <hi type="italic">strength</hi> in me. <hi type="super">7</hi> There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered for ever from my judge. <div eID="gen9810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> Job is confident that he has wrong done him by his friends, and therefore, ill as he is, he will not give up the cause, nor let them have the last word. Here, <div eID="gen9811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9812" type="x-p"/> I. He justifies his own resentments of his trouble (<reference osisRef="Job.23.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Even to day,</hi> I own, <hi type="italic">my complaint is bitter;</hi> for the affliction, the cause of the complaint, is so. There are <hi type="italic">wormwood and gall in the affliction and misery; my soul has them still in remembrance</hi> and is embittered by them, <reference osisRef="Lam.3.19-Lam.3.20">Lam. iii. 19, 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Even to day is my complaint</hi> counted <hi type="italic">rebellion</hi> (so some read it); his friends construed the innocent expressions of his grief into reflections upon God and his providence, and called them <hi type="italic">rebellion.</hi> "But," says he, "I do not complain more than there is cause; <hi type="italic">for my stroke is heavier than my groaning.</hi> Even today, after all you have said to convince and comfort me, still the pains of my body and the wounds of my spirit are such that I have reason enough for my complaints, if they were more bitter than they are." We wrong God if our groaning be heavier than our stroke, like froward children, who, when they cry for nothing, have justly something given them to cry for; but we do not wrong ourselves though our stroke be heavier than our groaning, for little said is soon amended. <div eID="gen9812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9813" type="x-p"/> II. He appeals from the censures of his friends to the just judgment of God; and this he thought was an evidence for him that he was not a hypocrite, for then he durst not have made such an appeal as this. St Paul comforted himself in this, that <hi type="italic">he that judged him was the Lord,</hi> and therefore he valued not man's judgment (<reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3-1Cor.4.4">1 Cor. iv. 3, 4</reference>), but he was willing to wait till the appointed day of decision came; whereas Job is impatient, and passionately wishes to have the judgment-day anticipated, and to have his cause tried quickly, as it were, by a special commission. The apostle found it necessary to press it much upon suffering Christians patiently to expect the Judge's coming, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.7-Jas.5.9">Jam. v. 7-9</reference>. <div eID="gen9813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> 1. He is so sure of the equity of God's tribunal that he longs to appear before it (<reference osisRef="Job.23.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">O that I knew where I might find him!</hi> This may properly express the pious breathings of a soul convinced that it has by sin lost God and is undone for ever if it recover not its interest in his favour. "O that I knew how I might recover his favour! How I might come into his covenant and communion with him!" <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.7">Mic. vi. 6, 7</reference>. It is the cry of a poor deserted soul. "<hi type="italic">Saw you him whom my soul loveth? O that I knew where I might find him!</hi> O that he who has laid open the way to himself would direct me into it and lead me in it!" But Job here seems to complain too boldly that his friends wronged him and he knew not which way to apply himself to God to have justice done him, else he would go even to his seat, to demand it. A patient waiting for death and judgment is our wisdom and duty, and, if we duly consider things, that cannot be without a holy fear and trembling; but a passionate wishing for death or judgment, without any such fear and trembling, is our sin and folly, and ill becomes us. Do we know what death and judgment are, and are we so very ready for them, that we need not time to get readier? <hi type="italic">Woe to those that</hi> thus, in a heat, <hi type="italic">desire the day of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Amos v. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen9814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9815" type="x-p"/> 2. He is so sure of the goodness of his own cause that he longs to be opening it at God's bar (<reference osisRef="Job.23.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I would order my cause before him,</hi> and set it in a true light. I would produce the evidences of my sincerity in a proper method, and would <hi type="italic">fill my mouth with arguments</hi> to prove it." We may apply this to the duty of prayer, in which we have <hi type="italic">boldness to enter into the holiest</hi> and to come even to the footstool of the throne of grace. We have not only liberty of access, but liberty of speech. We have leave, (1.) To be particular in our requests, <hi type="italic">to order our cause before God,</hi> to speak the whole matter, to lay before him all our grievances, in what method we think most proper; we durst not be so free with earthly princes as a humble holy soul may be with God. (2.) To be importunate in our requests. We are allowed, not only to pray, but to plead, not only to ask, but to argue; nay, to <hi type="italic">fill our mouths with arguments,</hi> not to move God (he is perfectly apprized of the merits of the cause without our showing), but to move ourselves, to excite our fervency and encourage our faith in prayer. <div eID="gen9815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9816" type="x-p"/> 3. He is so sure of a sentence in favour of him that he even longed to hear it (<reference osisRef="Job.23.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I would know the words which he would answer me,</hi>" that is, "I would gladly hear what God will say to this matter in dispute between you and me, and will entirely acquiesce in his judgment." This becomes us, in all controversies; let the word of God determine them; let us know what he answers, and understand what he says. Job knew well enough what his friends would answer him; they would condemn him, and run him down. "But" (says he) "<hi type="italic">I would</hi> fain <hi type="italic">know what God would answer me;</hi> for I am sure his judgment is according to truth, which theirs is not. I cannot understand them; they talk so little to the purpose. But what he says I should understand and therefore be fully satisfied in." <div eID="gen9816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9817" type="x-p"/> III. He comforts himself with the hope that God would deal favourably with him in this matter, <reference osisRef="Job.23.6-Job.23.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Note, It is of great use to us, in every thing wherein we have to do with God, to keep up good thoughts of him. He believes, 1. That God would not overpower him, that he would not deal with him either by absolute sovereignty or in strict justice, not with a high hand, nor with a strong hand: <hi type="italic">Will he plead against me with his great power?</hi> No. Job's friends pleaded against him with all the power they had; but will God do so? No; his power is all just and holy, whatever men's is. Against those that are obstinate in their unbelief and impenitency God will <hi type="italic">plead with his great power;</hi> their destruction will come <hi type="italic">from the glory of his power.</hi> But with his own people, that love him and trust in him, he will deal in tender compassion. 2. That, on the contrary, he would empower him to plead his own cause before God: "<hi type="italic">He would put strength in me,</hi> to support me and bear me up, in maintaining my integrity." Note, The same power that is engaged against proud sinners is engaged for humble saints, who prevail with God by strength derived from him, as Jacob did, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.3">Hos. xii. 3</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.68.35">Ps. lxviii. 35</reference>. 3. That the issue would certainly be comfortable, <reference osisRef="Job.23.7">v. 7</reference>. There, in the court of heaven, when the final sentence is to be given, <hi type="italic">the righteous might dispute with him</hi> and come off in his righteousness. Now, even the upright are often <hi type="italic">chastened of the Lord,</hi> and they cannot dispute against it; integrity itself is no fence either against calamity or calumny; but in that day <hi type="italic">they shall not be condemned with the world,</hi> though God may afflict by prerogative. <hi type="italic">Then you shall discern between the righteous and the wicked</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>), so vast will be the difference between them in their everlasting state; whereas now we can scarcely distinguish them, so little is the difference between them as to their outward condition, for all things come alike to all. Then, when the final doom is given, <hi type="italic">"I shall be delivered for ever from my Judge,</hi>" that is, "I shall be saved from the unjust censures of my friends and from that divine sentence which is now so much a terror to me." Those that are delivered up to God as their owner and ruler shall be for ever delivered from him as their judge and avenger; and there is no flying from his justice but by flying to his mercy.
entries.c237a8eacade97dc4302123ac3ecf656510fdb6d: <div eID="gen9817" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mystery of Providence. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Behold, I go forward, but he <hi type="italic">is</hi> not <hi type="italic">there;</hi> and backward, but I cannot perceive him: <hi type="super">9</hi> On the left hand, where he doth work, but I cannot behold <hi type="italic">him:</hi> he hideth himself on the right hand, that I cannot see <hi type="italic">him:</hi> 10 But he knoweth the way that I take: <hi type="italic">when</hi> he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold. <hi type="super">11</hi> My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined. <hi type="super">12</hi> Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary <hi type="italic">food.</hi> <div eID="gen9818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9819" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Job complains that he cannot understand the meaning of God's providences concerning him, but is quite at a loss about them (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I go forward, but he is not there,</hi> &c. Eliphaz had bid him acquaint himself with God. "So I would, with all my heart," says Job, "If I knew how to get acquainted with him." He had himself a great desire to appear before God, and get a hearing of his case, but the Judge was not to be found. Look which way he would, he could see no sign of God's appearing for him to clear up his innocency. Job, no doubt, believed that God is every where present; but three things he seems to complain of here:—1. That he could not fix his thoughts, nor form any clear judgment of things in his own mind. His mind was so hurried and discomposed with his troubles that he was like a man in a fright, or at his wits' end, who runs this way and that way, but, being in confusion, brings nothing to a head. By reason of the disorder and tumult his spirit was in he could not fasten upon that which he knew to be in God, and which, if he could but have mixed faith with it and dwelt upon it in his thoughts, would have been a support to him. It is the common complaint of those who are sick or melancholy that, when they would think of that which is good, they can make nothing of it. 2. That he could not find out the cause of his troubles, nor the sin which provoked God to contend with him. He took a view of his whole conversation, turned to every side of it, and could not perceive wherein he had sinned more than others, for which he should thus be punished more than others; nor could he discern what other end God should aim at in afflicting him thus. 3. That he could not foresee what would be in the end hereof, whether God would deliver him at all, nor, if he did, when or which way. He saw not his signs, nor was there any to tell him how long; as the church complains, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.9">Ps. lxxiv. 9</reference>. He was quite at a loss to know what God designed to do with him; and, whatever conjecture he advanced, still something or other appeared against it. <div eID="gen9819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9820" type="x-p"/> II. He satisfies himself with this, that God himself was a witness to his integrity, and therefore did not doubt but the issue would be good. <div eID="gen9820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9821" type="x-p"/> 1. After Job had almost lost himself in the labyrinth of the divine counsels, how contentedly does he sit down, at length, with this thought: "Though <hi type="italic">I</hi> know not the way that he takes (for <hi type="italic">his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters,</hi> his thoughts and ways are infinitely above ours and it would be presumption in us to pretend to judge of them), yet <hi type="italic">he knows the way that I take,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">v. 10</reference>. That is, (1.) He is acquainted with it. His friends judged of that which they did not know, and therefore charged him with that which he was never guilty of; but God, who knew every step he had taken, would not do so, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Ps. cxxxix. 3</reference>. Note, It is a great comfort to those who mean honestly that God understands their meaning, though men do not, cannot, or will not. (2.) He approves of it: "He knows that, however I may sometimes have <hi type="italic">taken a false step,</hi> yet I have still <hi type="italic">taken a good way,</hi> have <hi type="italic">chosen the way of truth,</hi> and therefore he knows it," that is, he accepts it, and is well pleased with it, as he is said to <hi type="italic">know the way of the righteous,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Ps. i. 6</reference>. This comforted the prophet, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.3">Jer. xii. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thou hast tried my heart towards thee.</hi> From this Job infers, <hi type="italic">When he hath tried me I shall come forth as gold.</hi> Those that <hi type="italic">keep the way of the Lord</hi> may comfort themselves, when they are in affliction, with these three things:—[1.] That they are but tried. It is not intended for their hurt, but for their honour and benefit; <hi type="italic">it is the trial of their faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 7</reference>. [2.] That, when they are sufficiently tried, they shall come forth out of the furnace, and not be left to consume in it as dross or reprobate silver. The trial will have an end. <hi type="italic">God will not contend for ever.</hi> [3.] That they shall come forth as gold, pure in itself and precious to the refiner. They shall come forth as gold approved and improved, found to be good and made to be better. Afflictions are to us as we are; those that go gold into the furnace will come out no worse. <div eID="gen9821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9822" type="x-p"/> 2. Now that which encouraged Job to hope that his present troubles would thus end well was the testimony of his conscience for him, that he had lived a good life in the fear of God. <div eID="gen9822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9823" type="x-p"/> (1.) That God's way was the way he walked in (<reference osisRef="Job.23.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My foot hath held his steps,</hi>" that is, "held to them, adhered closely to them; the steps he takes. I have endeavoured to conform myself to his example." Good people are followers of God. Or, "I have accommodated myself to his providence, and endeavoured to answer all the intentions of that, to follow Providence step by step." Or, "His steps are the steps he has appointed me to take; the way of religion and serious godliness—that way I have kept, and have not declined from it, not only not turned back from it by a total apostasy, but not turned aside out of it by any wilful transgression." His holding God's steps, and keeping his way, intimate that the tempter had used all his arts by fraud and force to draw him aside; but, with care and resolution, he had by the grace of God hitherto persevered, and those that will do so must hold and keep, hold with resolution and keep with watchfulness. <div eID="gen9823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9824" type="x-p"/> (2.) That God's word was the rule he walked by, <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">v. 12</reference>. He governed himself by <hi type="italic">the commandment of God's lips,</hi> and would not go back from that, but go forward according to it. Whatever difficulties we may meet with in the way of God's commandments, though they lead us through a wilderness, yet we must never think of going back, but must press on towards the mark. Job kept closely to the law of God in his conversation, for both his judgment and his affection led him to it: <hi type="italic">I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food;</hi> that is, he looked upon it as his necessary food; he could as well have lived without his daily bread as without the word of God. <hi type="italic">I have laid it up</hi> (so the word is), as those that lay up provision for a siege, or as Joseph laid up corn before the famine. Eliphaz had told him to <hi type="italic">lay up God's words in his heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.22">ch. xxii. 22</reference>. "I do," says he, "and always did, <hi type="italic">that I might not sin against him,</hi> and that, like the good householder, I might bring forth for the good of others." Note, The word of God is to our souls what our necessary food is to our bodies; it sustains the spiritual life and strengthens us for the actions of life; it is that which we cannot subsist without, and which nothing else can make up the want of: and we ought therefore so to esteem it, to take pains for it, hunger after it, feed upon it with delight, and nourish our souls with it; and this will be our rejoicing in the day of evil, as it was Job's here.
entries.807a16e8aa67b53ccb0935d4aa01c201bcdd79e6: <div eID="gen9824" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Comfort in His Integrity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9825" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> But he <hi type="italic">is</hi> in one <hi type="italic">mind,</hi> and who can turn him? and <hi type="italic">what</hi> his soul desireth, even <hi type="italic">that</hi> he doeth. <hi type="super">14</hi> For he performeth <hi type="italic">the thing that is</hi> appointed for me: and many such <hi type="italic">things are</hi> with him. <hi type="super">15</hi> Therefore am I troubled at his presence: when I consider, I am afraid of him. <hi type="super">16</hi> For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me: <hi type="super">17</hi> Because I was not cut off before the darkness, <hi type="italic">neither</hi> hath he covered the darkness from my face. <div eID="gen9825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9826" type="x-p"/> Some make Job to complain here that God dealt unjustly and unfairly with him in proceeding to punish him without the least relenting or relaxation, though he had such incontestable evidences to produce of his innocency. I am loth to think holy Job would charge the holy God with iniquity; but his complaint is indeed bitter and peevish, and he reasons himself into a sort of <hi type="italic">patience per force,</hi> which he cannot do without reflecting upon God as dealing hardly with him, but he must bear it because he cannot help it; the worst he says is that God deals unaccountably with him. <div eID="gen9826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9827" type="x-p"/> I. He lays down good truths, and truths which were capable of a good improvement, <reference osisRef="Job.23.13-Job.23.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. 1. That God's counsels are immutable: <hi type="italic">He is in one mind, and who can turn him? He is one</hi> (so some read it) or <hi type="italic">in one;</hi> he has no counsellors by whose interest he might be prevailed with to alter his purpose: he is one with himself, and never alters his mind, never alters his measures. Prayer has prevailed to change God's way and his providence, but never was his will or purpose changed; for <hi type="italic">known unto God are all his works.</hi> 2. That his power is irresistible: <hi type="italic">What his soul desires</hi> or designs <hi type="italic">even that he does,</hi> and nothing can stand in his way or put him upon new counsels. Men desire many things which they may not do, or cannot do, or dare not do. But God has an incontestable sovereignty; his will is so perfectly pure and right that it is highly fit he should pursue all its determinations. And he has an uncontrollable power. <hi type="italic">None can stay his hand. Whatever the Lord pleased that did he</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.135.6">Ps. cxxxv. 6</reference>), and always will, for it is always best. 3. That all he does is according to the counsel of his will (<reference osisRef="Job.23.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">He performs the thing that is appointed for me.</hi> Whatever happens to us, it is God that performs it (<reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Ps. lvii. 2</reference>), and an admirable performance the whole will appear to be when the mystery of God shall be finished. He performs all that, and that only, which was appointed, and in the appointed time and method. This may silence us, for what is appointed cannot be altered. But to consider that, when God was appointing us to eternal life and glory as our end, he was appointing to this condition, this affliction, whatever it is, in our way, this may do more than silence us, it may satisfy us that it is all for the best; though what he does we know not now, yet we shall know hereafter. 4. That all he does is according to the custom of his providence: <hi type="italic">Many such things are with him,</hi> that is, He does many things in the course of his providence which we can give no account of, but must resolve into his absolute sovereignty. Whatever trouble we are in others have been in the like. Our case is not singular; the same <hi type="italic">afflictions are accomplished in our brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.9">1 Pet. v. 9</reference>. Are we sick or sore, impoverished and stripped? Are our children removed by death or our friends unkind? This is what <hi type="italic">God has appointed for us, and many such things are with him. Shall the earth be forsaken for us?</hi> <div eID="gen9827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9828" type="x-p"/> II. He makes but a bad use of these good truths. Had he duly considered them, he might have said, "Therefore am I easy and pleased, and well reconciled to the way of my God concerning me; therefore will I rejoice in hope that my troubles will issue well at last." But he said, <hi type="italic">Therefore am I troubled at his presence,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.15">v. 15</reference>. Those are indeed of troubled spirits who are troubled at the presence of God, as the psalmist, who <hi type="italic">remembered God and was troubled,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.3">Ps. lxxvii. 3</reference>. See what confusion poor Job was now in, for he contradicted himself: just now he was troubled for God's absence (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.9">v. 8, 9</reference>); now he is troubled at his presence. <hi type="italic">When I consider, I am afraid of him.</hi> What he now felt made him fear worse. There is indeed that which, if we consider it, will show that we have cause to be afraid of God—his infinite justice and purity, compared with our own sinfulness and vileness; but if, withal, we consider his grace in a Redeemer, and our compliance with that grace, our fears will vanish and we shall see cause to hope in him. See what impressions were made upon him by the wounds of his spirit. 1. He was very fearful (<reference osisRef="Job.23.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Almighty troubled him,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">made his heart soft,</hi> that is, utterly unable to bear any thing, and afraid of every thing that stirred. There is a gracious softness, like that of Josiah, whose heart was tender, and trembled at the word of God; but this is meant of a grievous softness which apprehends every thing that is present to be pressing and every thing future to be threatening. 2. He was very fretful, peevish indeed, for he quarrels with God, (1.) Because he did not die before his troubles, that he might never have seen them (<hi type="italic">Because I was not cut off before the darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.17">v. 17</reference>), and yet if, in the height of his prosperity, he had received a summons to the grave, he would have thought it hard. This may help to reconcile us to death, whenever it comes, that we do not know what evil we may be taken away from. But when trouble comes it is folly to wish we had not lived to see it and it is better to make the best of it. (2.) Because he was left to live so long in his troubles, and the darkness was not covered from his face by his being hidden in the grave. We should bear the darkness better than thus if we would but remember that to the upright there sometimes arises a marvellous light in the darkness; however, there is reserved for them a more marvellous light after it.  <chapter eID="Job.23"/> <div eID="gen9828" type="x-p"/>

entries.3949991af19484005636e6c5abf6ccbc2f395f49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4959"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen7307" type="x-p"/> THIRD SERIES.<div eID="gen7307" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Job.23.1-Job.23.17">Job 23:1-17</reference>. Job's Answer.</title> <div sID="gen7308" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4959"/><hi type="bold">2. to-day--</hi>implying, perhaps, that the debate was carried on through more days than one (see Introduction).<div eID="gen7308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bitter--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">10:1</reference>).<div eID="gen7309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my stroke--</hi>the hand of God on me (Margin, <reference osisRef="Job.19.21">Job 19:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.4">Psa 32:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavier than--</hi>is so heavy that I cannot relieve myself adequately by groaning. <div eID="gen7311" type="x-p"/>
entries.026c5a9ae530b2c05449d52f206070dd28be831b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4960"/><div sID="gen7312" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4960"/>3. The same wish as in <reference osisRef="Job.13.3">Job 13:3</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.10.19-Heb.10.22">He 10:19-22</reference>).<div eID="gen7312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Seat--</hi>The idea in the Hebrew is a well-prepared throne (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.7">Psa 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7313" type="x-p"/>
entries.c87b8aa4d27216ff667f63b8972b680bc4b4178d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4961"/><div sID="gen7314" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4961"/><hi type="bold">4. order--</hi>state methodically (<reference osisRef="Job.13.18">Job 13:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Is 43:26</reference>).<div eID="gen7314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fill, &c.--</hi>I would have abundance of arguments to adduce. <div eID="gen7315" type="x-p"/>
entries.9af19cfea451e86fd90e6f98ae7a60194c887dc1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4962"/><div sID="gen7316" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4962"/><hi type="bold">5. he--</hi>emphatic: it little matters what man may say of me, if only I know what God judges of me. <div eID="gen7316" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7732f9fd3aa9d8cafa79bca81033e052f5982b9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4963"/><div sID="gen7317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4963"/>6. An objection suggests itself, while he utters the wish (<reference osisRef="Job.23.5">Job 23:5</reference>). Do I hereby wish that He should plead against me with His omnipotence? Far from it! (<reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job 9:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">13:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.18">30:18</reference>).<div eID="gen7317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strength--</hi>so as to prevail with Him: as in Jacob's case (<reference osisRef="Hos.12.3">Ho 12:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">4</reference>). Umbreit and Maurer better translate as in <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference> (I only wish that He) "would attend to me," that is, give me a patient hearing as an ordinary judge, not using His omnipotence, but only His divine knowledge of my innocence. <div eID="gen7318" type="x-p"/>
entries.88b10c69fdc86f0258a57d935d313abea4898e2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4964"/><div sID="gen7319" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4964"/><hi type="bold">7. There--</hi>rather, "Then": if God would "attend" to me (<reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen7319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteous--</hi>that is, the result of my dispute would be, He would acknowledge me as righteous.<div eID="gen7320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered--</hi>from suspicion of guilt on the part of my Judge. <div eID="gen7321" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2308bc3deaf4bb40f1ce7d2102930adcfd3845a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4965"/><div sID="gen7322" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4965"/>8. But I wish in vain. For "behold," &c.<div eID="gen7322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forward ... backward--</hi>rather, "to the east--to the west." The Hebrew geographers faced the east, that is, sunrise: not the north, as we do. So "before" means east: "behind," west (so the Hindus). Para, "before"--east: Apara, "behind"--west: Daschina, "the right hand"--south: Bama, "left"--north. A similar reference to sunrise appears in the name Asia, "sunrise," Europe, "sunset"; pure Babylonian names, as Rawlinson shows. <div eID="gen7323" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f832fc5d202d405a6cb4a0dd2d01153f567c6ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4966"/><div sID="gen7324" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4966"/>9. Rather, "To the north."<div eID="gen7324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">work--</hi>God's glorious works are especially seen towards the north region of the sky by one in the northern hemisphere. The antithesis is between God working and yet not being beheld: as in <reference osisRef="Job.9.11">Job 9:11</reference>, between "He goeth by," and "I see Him not." If the Hebrew bears it, the parallelism to the second clause is better suited by translating, as Umbreit, "doth hide himself"; but then the antithesis to "behold" would be lost.<div eID="gen7325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right hand--</hi>"in the south."<div eID="gen7326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hideth--</hi>appropriately, of the unexplored south, then regarded as uninhabitable because of its heat (see <reference osisRef="Job.34.29">Job 34:29</reference>). <div eID="gen7327" type="x-p"/>
entries.9db816604a3c5de675cb2d2fc05e79cb75a030a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4967"/><div sID="gen7328" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4967"/><hi type="bold">10. But--</hi>correcting himself for the wish that his cause should be known before God. The omniscient One already knoweth the way in me (my inward principles: His outward way or course of acts is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>. So in me, <reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>); though for some inscrutable cause He as yet hides Himself (<reference osisRef="Job.23.8">Job 23:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.23.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen7328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when--</hi>let Him only but try my cause, I shall, &c. <div eID="gen7329" type="x-p"/>
entries.030eb1cfdb0022289847ca441351919aac986974: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4968"/><div sID="gen7330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4968"/><hi type="bold">11. held--</hi>fast by His steps. The law is in Old Testament poetry regarded as a way, God going before us as our guide, in whose footsteps we must tread (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>).<div eID="gen7330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">declined--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">Psa 125:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7331" type="x-p"/>
entries.4ec9c70efb0ca65a026eaadc7bda521b0cae3647: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4969"/><div sID="gen7332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4969"/><hi type="bold">12. esteemed--</hi>rather, "laid up," namely, as a treasure found (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Psa 119:11</reference>); alluding to the words of Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.22.22">Job 22:22</reference>). There was no need to tell me so; I have done so already (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.16">Jr 15:16</reference>).<div eID="gen7332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">necessary--</hi>"Appointed portion" (of food; as in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.8">Pr 30:8</reference>). Umbreit and Maurer translate, "More than my law," my own will, in antithesis to "the words of His mouth" (<reference osisRef="John.6.38">Joh 6:38</reference>). Probably under the general term, "what is appointed to me" (the same Hebrew is in <reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference>), all that ministers to the appetites of the body and carnal will is included. <div eID="gen7333" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b51731a87b7c01d9b378ab28d94859ad74446a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4970"/><div sID="gen7334" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4970"/><hi type="bold">13. in one mind--</hi>notwithstanding my innocence, He is unaltered in His purpose of proving me guilty (<reference osisRef="Job.9.12">Job 9:12</reference>).<div eID="gen7334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">soul--</hi>His will (<reference osisRef="Ps.115.3">Psa 115:3</reference>). God's sovereignty. He has one great purpose; nothing is haphazard; everything has its proper place with a view to His purpose. <div eID="gen7335" type="x-p"/>
entries.8f6648cd46cd6c7d6389b70cf8a55fc94345dca1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4971"/><div sID="gen7336" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4971"/><hi type="bold">14. many such--</hi>He has yet many more such ills in store for me, though hidden in His breast (<reference osisRef="Job.10.13">Job 10:13</reference>). <div eID="gen7336" type="x-p"/>
entries.78abc58636827dbe890f91cada0a30e648060ab7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4972"/><div sID="gen7337" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4972"/>15. God's decrees, impossible to be resisted, and leaving us in the dark as to what may come next, are calculated to fill the mind with holy awe [Barnes]. <div eID="gen7337" type="x-p"/>
entries.1941f8e0d3c3cf9ea9882fcbd6c351e0e6916a25: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4973"/><div sID="gen7338" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4973"/><hi type="bold">16. soft--</hi>faint; hath melted my courage. Here again Job's language is that of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Psa 22:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7338" type="x-p"/>
entries.c8af7dc31baed56aa9353a11f2af9e77cfe9a8f8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4974"/><div sID="gen7339" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4974"/>17. Because I was not taken away by death from the evil to come (literally, "from before the face of the darkness," <reference osisRef="Isa.57.1">Is 57:1</reference>). Alluding to the words of Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.22.11">Job 22:11</reference>), "darkness," that is, calamity.<div eID="gen7339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>rather, in the Arabic sense, brought to the land of silence; my sad complaint hushed in death [Umbreit]. "Darkness" in the second clause, not the same Hebrew word as in the first, "cloud," "obscurity." Instead of "covering the cloud (of evil) from my face," He "covers" me with it (<reference osisRef="Job.22.11">Job 22:11</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.23"/>

entries.459623718ec65aff471cb971b10356e67eaabeb7: <div eID="gen17000" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17001" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17002" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17002" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17001" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17003" type="x-p"/> Job answers; apologizes for his complaining; wishes to plead his cause in the presence of his Maker, from whom he knows he should receive justice; but regrets that he cannot find him, <reference osisRef="Job.23.1-Job.23.9">Job 23:1-9</reference>. He, however, gives himself and his cause up to God, with the conviction of his own innocence, and God's justice and goodness, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10-Job.23.14">Job 23:10-14</reference>. He is, nevertheless, afraid when he considers the majesty of his Maker, <reference osisRef="Job.23.15-Job.23.17">Job 23:15-17</reference>.
entries.5cc527275e5eb87aeadac51fac8d9767a4650f76: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17004" type="x-p"/> Even to-day is my complaint bitter - Job goes on to maintain his own innocence, and shows that he has derived neither conviction nor consolation from the discourses of his friends. He grants that his complaint is bitter; but states that, loud as it may be, the affliction which he endures is heavier than his complaints are loud. Mr. Good translates: "And still is my complaint rebellion?" Do ye construe my lamentations over my unparalleled sufferings as rebellion against God? This, in fact, they had done from the beginning: and the original will justify the version of Mr. Good; for מרי meri, which we translate bitter, may be derived from מרה marah, "he rebelled."
entries.b7e237b83ad5fc731b543a076981b68730629d23: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17005" type="x-p"/> O that I knew where I might find him! - This and the following verse may be read thus: "Who will give me the knowledge of God, that I may find him out? I would come to his establishment; (the place or way in which he has promised to communicate himself); I would exhibit, in detail, my judgment (the cause I wish to be tried) before his face; and my mouth would I fill with convincing or decisive arguments;" arguments drawn from his common method of saving sinners, which I should prove applied fully to my case. Hence the confidence with which he speaks, <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference>.
entries.90fcdc320b891e648e9ddc00b3807e62997acb11: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17006" type="x-p"/> I would know the words which he would answer me - He would speak nothing but what was true, decree nothing that was not righteous, nor utter any thing that I could not comprehend.
entries.5757c827cdf4230ec3426300bbe9906eef98f5ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17007" type="x-p"/> Will he plead against me - He would not exhibit his majesty and his sovereign authority to strike me dumb, or so overawe me that I could not speak in my own vindication. <div eID="gen17007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17008" type="x-p"/> No; but he would put strength in me - On the contrary, he would treat me with tenderness, he would rectify my mistakes, he would show me what was in my favor, and would temper the rigid demands of justice by the mild interpretations of equity; and where law could not clear me, mercy would conduct all to the most favorable issue.
entries.1a8a70f0cba00bec71067525c8fe4acff12face0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17009" type="x-p"/> There the righteous might dispute with him - נוכח nochach, might argue or plead. To dispute with God sounds very harsh. <div eID="gen17009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17010" type="x-p"/> So should I be delivered for ever - Mr. Good translates: "And triumphantly should I escape from my condemnation." The Hebrew word לנצח lanetsach may as well be translated to victory as for ever: and in this sense the Vulgate understood the words: Proponat aequitatem contra me; et perveniat ad victoriam judicium meum. "He would set up equity against me; and would lead on my cause to victory." Coverdale renders thus: - But let hym give me like power to go to lawe, then am I sure to wynne my matter. Nothing less than the fullest conviction of his own innocence could have led Job to express himself thus to the Judge of quick and dead!
entries.4111c175ba954fab850ee503dab439b4fd61372f: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17011" type="x-p"/> Behold, I go forward - These two verses paint in vivid colors the distress and anxiety of a soul in search of the favor of God. No means are left untried, no place unexplored, in order to find the object of his research. This is a true description of the conduct of a genuine penitent.
entries.373021c762320345ba4d65fae8d1262057671f4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17012" type="x-p"/> On the left hand, where he doth work - In these two verses Job mentions the four cardinal points of the heavens: the East, by the word קדם kedem, which signifies before; the West, by אחור achor, which signifies after, or the back part; the North, by שמאל semol, which signifies the left; and the South, by ימין yamin, which signifies the right. Such is the situation of the world to a man who faces the east; see <reference osisRef="Gen.13.9">Gen 13:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.11">Gen 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.28.14">Gen 28:14</reference>. And from this it appears that the Hebrews, Idumeans, and Arabs had the same ideas of these points of the heavens. It is worthy of remark that Job says, He hideth himself on the right hand, (the south), that I cannot see him: for in fact, the southern point of heaven is not visible in Idumea, where Job was. Hence it comes that when he spake before, <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>, of the constellations of the antarctic pole, he terms them the hidden chambers of the south; i.e., those compartments of the celestial concave that never appeared above the horizon in that place - See Calmet. <div eID="gen17012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17013" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good translates these verses as follows: - <div eID="gen17013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17014" type="x-p"/> Behold! I go forward, and he is not there; <div eID="gen17014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17015" type="x-p"/> And backward, but I cannot perceive him. <div eID="gen17015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17016" type="x-p"/> On the left hand I feel for him, but trace him not: <div eID="gen17016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17017" type="x-p"/> He enshroudeth the right hand, and I cannot see him. <div eID="gen17017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17018" type="x-p"/> The simple rendering of Coverdale is nervous and correct: - <div eID="gen17018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17019" type="x-p"/> For though I go before, I fynde hym not: <div eID="gen17019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17020" type="x-p"/> Yf I come behynde, I can get no knowledge of him: <div eID="gen17020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17021" type="x-p"/> Yf I go on the left syde to pondre his workes, <div eID="gen17021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17022" type="x-p"/> I cannot atteyne unto them: <div eID="gen17022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17023" type="x-p"/> Agayne, yf I go on the right syde, he hydeth himself, <div eID="gen17023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17024" type="x-p"/> That I cannot se him.
entries.eb7d6255a1b30f7c58d276dc37616f090312e719: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17025" type="x-p"/> But he knoweth the way that I take - He approves of my conduct; my ways please him. He tries me: but, like gold, I shall lose nothing in the fire; I shall come forth more pure and luminous. If that which is reputed to be gold is exposed to the action of a strong fire, if it be genuine, it will lose nothing of its quality, nor of its weight. If it went into the fire gold, it will come out gold; the strongest fire will neither alter nor destroy it. So Job: he went into this furnace of affliction an innocent, righteous man; he came out the same. His character lost nothing of its value, nothing of its lustre.
entries.6d26faa67c243d827309892820d54a6f4f48c0e9: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17026" type="x-p"/> My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept - I have carefully marked his providential dealings; and in his way - his pure and undefiled religion - have I walked. I have not only been generally but particularly religious: I have attended carefully to the weightier matters of the law, and have not forgotten its slightest injunctions. <div eID="gen17026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17027" type="x-p"/> Coverdale is curious: - Nevertheles my fete kepe his path, his hye strete have I holden, and not gone out of it. The hye strete is highway, the causeway, or raised road; formed, as they anciently were, by stones in the manner of pavement. It has its name from the Latin strata, paved, via being understood: via lapidibus strata, "a way paved with stones:" hence street, a raised road or pavement either in town or country. And hence the four grand Roman or British roads which intersected this kingdom: viz. Watling street, Icknild or Ricknild street, Ermin street, and Fosse street. Some say these streets or roads were made by Bellinus, a British king. Fosse street began in Cornwall, passed through Devonshire, Somersetshire, and along by Titbury upon Toteswould, beside Coventry, unto Leicester; and thence by the wide plains to Newark and to Lincoln, where it ends. Watling street begins at Dover, passes through the middle of Kent, over the Thames by London, running near Westminster, and thence to St. Alban's, Dunstable, Stratford, Towcester, Weden, Lilbourn, Atherston, Wreaken by Severn, Worcester, Stratton, through Wales unto Cardigan, and on to the Irish sea. Ermin, or Erminage street, running from St. David's in Wales, to Southampton. Ricknild, or Icknild street, running by Worcester, Wycomb, Birmingham, Lichfield, Derby, Chesterfield, and by York, into Tynemouth. See Camden, Holinshed, and Minshieu.
entries.48fb5aaa2646feb4d42c8d973e5d1d19355aee09: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17028" type="x-p"/> The commandment of his lips - The written law that proceeded from his own mouth. <div eID="gen17028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17029" type="x-p"/> I have esteemed the words of his mouth - Mr. Good has given a better version of the original: In my bosom have I stored up the words of his mouth. The Asiatics carry every thing precious or valuable in their bosom, their handkerchiefs, jewels, purses, etc. Job, therefore, intimates that the words of God's mouth were to him a most precious treasure.
entries.e5f0ca71248491499f4c8926c92b86b615934dfd: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17030" type="x-p"/> But he is in one mind - The original is והוא באחד vehu beechad, and is literally, But he is in one: properly rendered by the Vulgate, Ipse enim solus est. But he is alone. And not badly rendered by Coverdale - It is he himself alone. He has no partner; his designs are his own, they are formed in his infinite wisdom, and none can turn his determinations aside. It is vain, therefore, for man to contend with his Maker. He designs my happiness, and you cannot prevent its accomplishment.
entries.aa0ef7251059c534e1d8b86672aab59025970a77: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17031" type="x-p"/> For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me - Coverdale translates: - He rewardeth me into my bosome, and many other thinges mo doth he, as he maye by his power. חקי chukki may as well be translated bosom here as in <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference>; but probably it may mean a portion, lot, sufficiency: For he hath appointed me my lot; and like these there are multitudes with him. He diversifies human affairs: scarcely any two men have the same lot; nor has the same person the same portion at all times. He has multitudes of resources, expedients, means, etc., which he employs in governing human affairs.
entries.053498add986b29e141ce9889befa19acc333362: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17032" type="x-p"/> Therefore am I troubled - I do not as yet see an end to my afflictions: he has not exhausted his means of trial; therefore, when I consider this, I am afraid of him.
entries.8f4533cd99528ef682d05194ffef361436c1e32e: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17033" type="x-p"/> For God maketh my heart soft - Prostrates my strength, deprives me of courage, so that I sink beneath my burden, and I am troubled at the thought of the Almighty, the self-sufficient and eternal Being.
entries.33640b47c5bc3ca94bb639f52aa35b0439de2ef9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17034" type="x-p"/> Because I was not cut off - "O, why can I not draw darkness over my face? Why may not thick darkness cover my face?" Mr. Good. This verse should be read in connection with the preceding; and then we shall have the following sense. <reference osisRef="Job.23.16">Job 23:16</reference> : "The Lord hath beaten down my strength, and my soul has been terrified by his fear." <reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference> : "For it is not this deep night in which I am enveloped, nor the evils which I suffer, that have overwhelmed me; I sink only through the fear which the presence of his Majesty inspires. This is my greatest affliction; sufferings, diseases, yea, death itself, are nothing in comparison of the terror which my soul feels in the presence of his tremendous holiness and justice." <div eID="gen17034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17035" type="x-p"/> Nothing can humble a pious mind so much as Scriptural apprehensions of the majesty of God. It is easy to contemplate his goodness, loving-kindness, and mercy; in all these we have an interest, and from them we expect the greatest good: but to consider his holiness and justice, the infinite righteousness of his nature, under the conviction that we have sinned, and broken the laws prescribed by his sovereign Majesty, and to feel ourselves brought as into the presence of his judgment-seat, - who can bear the thought? If cherubim and seraphim veil their faces before his throne, and the holiest soul exclaims, <div eID="gen17035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17036" type="x-p"/> I loathe myself when God I see, <div eID="gen17036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17037" type="x-p"/> And into nothing fall; what must a sinner feel, whose conscience is not yet purged from dead works and who feels the wrath of God abiding on him? And how without such a mediator and sacrifice as Jesus Christ is, can any human spirit come into the presence of its Judge? Those who can approach him without terror, know little of his justice and nothing of their sin. When we approach him in prayer, or in any ordinance, should we not feel more reverence than we generally do?  <chapter eID="Job.23"/> <div eID="gen17037" type="x-p"/>

entries.78b6434ce13cc2713370c383fdd7d7bc7a2bb42d: <reference osisRef="Job.23.1-Job.5.1">Job 23:1-5   1</reference>  Then began Job, and said:   2  Even to-day my complaint still biddeth defiance, <div eID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> My hand lieth heavy upon my groaning.   3  Oh that I knew where I might find Him, <div eID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> That I might come even to His dwelling-place!   4  I would lay the cause before Him, <div eID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> And fill my mouth with arguments:   5  I should like to know the words He would answer me, <div eID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> And attend to what He would say to me. <div eID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> Since מרי (for which the lxx reads ἐκ τοῦ χειρός μου, מידי; Ew. מידו, from his hand) usually elsewhere signifies obstinacy, it appears that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> ought to be explained: My complaint is always accounted as rebellion (against God); but by this rendering <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> requires some sort of expletive, in order to furnish a connected thought: <hi type="italic">although</hi> the hand which is upon me stifles my groaning (Hirz.); or, according to another rendering of the על: <hi type="italic">et pourtant mes gémissements n'égalent pas mes souffrances </hi>(Renan. Schlottm.). These interpretations are objectionable on account of the artificial restoration of the connection between the two members of the verse, which they require; they lead one to expect וידי (as a circumstantial clause: lxx, <hi type="italic">Cod. Vat.</hi> καὶ ἡ χεὶρ αὐτοῦ). As the words stand, it is to be supposed that the definition of time, גּם־היּום (even to-day still, as Zec 9:12), belongs to both divisions of the verse. How, then, is מרי to be understood? If we compare <reference osisRef="Job.7.11">Job 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.10.1">Job 10:1</reference>, where מר, which is combined with שׂיח, signifies <hi type="italic">amarum</hi> = <hi type="italic">amartiduo</hi>, it is natural to take מרי also in the signification <hi type="italic">amaritudo, acerbitas</hi> (Targ., Syr., Jer.); and this is also possible, since, as is evident from <reference osisRef="Exod.23.21">Exo 23:21</reference>, comp. Zec 12:10, the verbal forms מרר and מרה run into one another, as they are really cognates.<note placement="foot">מרר and מרה both spring from the root מר [<hi type="italic">vid. supra,</hi> p. 396, note], with the primary signification <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, to beat, rub, draw tight. Hence Arab. <hi type="italic">mârrâ</hi>, to touch lightly, smear upon (to go by, over, or through, to move by, etc.), but also <hi type="italic">stringere palatum,</hi> of an astringent taste, strong in taste, to be bitter, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥalâ</hi>, soft and mild in taste, to be sweet, as in another direction חלה, to be loose, weak, sick, both from the root Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥl</hi> in <hi type="italic">ḥalla , solvit, laxavit.</hi> From the signification to be tight come <hi type="italic">amarra</hi>, to stretch tight, <hi type="italic">istamarra</hi>, to stretch one’s self tight, to draw one’s self out in this state of tension - of things in time, to continue unbroken; <hi type="italic">mirreh</hi>, string, cord; מרה, to make and hold one’s self tight against any one, i.e., to be obstinate: originally of the body, as Arab. <hi type="italic">mârrâ , tamârrâ</hi>, to strengthen themselves in the contest against one another; then of the mind, as Arab. <hi type="italic">mârâ , tamârâ ,</hi> to struggle against anything, both outwardly by contradiction and disputing, and inwardly by doubt and unbelief. - Fl.</note> <div eID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> But it is more satisfactory, and more in accordance with the relation of the two divisions of the verse, if we keep to the usual signification of מרי; not, however, understanding it of obstinacy, revolt, rebellion (viz., in the sense of the friends), but, like moreh, 2Ki 14:26) which describes the affliction as stiff-necked, obstinate), of stubbornness, defiance, continuance in opposition, and explain with Raschi: My complaint is still always defiance, i.e., still maintains itself in opposition, viz., against God, without yielding (Hahn, Olsh.: unsubmitting); or rather: against such exhortations to penitence as those which Eliphaz has just addressed to him. In reply to these, Job considers his complain to be well justified even to-day, i.e., even now (for it is not, with Ewald, to be imagined that, in the mind of the poet, the controversy extends over several days, - an idea which would only be indicated by this one word). <div eID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> he continues the same thought under a different form of expression. My hand lies heavy on my groaning, i.e., I hold it immoveably fast (as Fleischer proposes to take the words); or better: I am driven to a continued utterance of it.<note placement="foot">The idea might also be: My hand presses my groaning back (because it would be of no use to me); but <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> is against this, and the Arab. <hi type="italic">kamada</hi>, to restrain inward pain, anger, etc. by force (e.g., <hi type="italic">mât kemed ,</hi> he died from suppressed rage or anxiety), has scarcely any etymological connection with כבד.</note> <div eID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> By this interpretation ydy retains its most natural meaning, <hi type="italic">manus mea,</hi> and the connection of the two members of the verse without any particle is best explained. On the other hand, all modern expositors, who do not, as Olsh., at once correct ידי into ידו, explain the suffix as objective: the hand, i.e., the destiny to which I have to submit, weighs upon my sighing, irresistibly forcing it out from me. Then <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> is related to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.2">Job 23:2</reference></hi> as a confirmation; and if, therefore, a particle is to be supplied, it is כּי (Olsh.) and no other. Thus, even the Targ. renders it machatiy, <hi type="italic">plaga mea.</hi> Job’s affliction is frequently traced back to the hand of God, <reference osisRef="Job.19.21">Job 19:21</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.1.11">Job 1:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.2.5">Job 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">Job 13:21</reference>; and on the suffix used objectively (pass.) we may compare <reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference>, חקּי; <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference>, אמרו; and especially <reference osisRef="Job.34.6">Job 34:6</reference>, חצּי. The interpretation: the hand upon me is heavy above my sighing, i.e., heavier than it (Ramban, Rosenm., Ges., Schlottm., Renan), also accords with the connection. על can indeed be used in this comparative meaning, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.5">Exo 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.16">Ecc 1:16</reference>; but כבדה יד על is an established phrase, and commonly used of the burden of the hand upon any one, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.4">Psa 32:4</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.33.7">Job 33:7</reference>, in the division in which Elihu is introduced; and the connection with אל,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.6">1Sa 5:6</reference>, and שׁם,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.11">1Sa 5:11</reference>); and this usage of the language renders the comparative rendering very improbable. But it is also improbable that “my hand” is = the hand that is upon me, since it cannot be shown that יד was directly used in the sense of <hi type="italic">plaga;</hi> even the Arabic, among the many turns of meaning which it gives to Arab. <hi type="italic">yd ,</hi> does not support this, and least of all would an Arab conceive of Arab. <hi type="italic">ydâ</hi> passively, <hi type="italic">plaga quam patior. </hi> Explain, therefore: his complain now, as before, offers resistance to the exhortation of the friends, which is not able to lessen it, his (Job’s) hand presses upon his lamentation so that it is forced to break forth, but - without its justification being recognised by men. This thought urges him on to the wish that he might be able to pour forth his complain directly before God. מי־יתּן is at one time followed by an accusative (<reference osisRef="Job.14.4">Job 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.2">Job 29:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.35">Job 31:35</reference>, to which belongs also the construction with the inf., <reference osisRef="Job.11.5">Job 11:5</reference>), at another by the <hi type="italic">fut.,</hi> with or without <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> (as here, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.6.8">Job 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.5">Job 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">Job 19:23</reference>), and at another by the <hi type="italic">perf.,</hi> with or without <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> (as here, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.3">Job 23:3</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">utinam noverim,</hi> and <reference osisRef="Deut.5.26">Deu 5:26</reference>). And ידעתּי is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.32.22">Job 32:22</reference>, joined with the <hi type="italic">fut.: scirem</hi> (<hi type="italic">noverim</hi>) <hi type="italic">et invenirem</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">possim invenire eum</hi> (למצאו), Ges. §142, 3, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. If he but knew how to reach Him (God), could attain to His throne; תּכוּנה (everywhere from כּוּן, not from תּכן) signifies the setting up, i.e., arrangement (<reference osisRef="Ezek.43.11">Eze 43:11</reference>) or establishment (<reference osisRef="Nah.2.10">Nah 2:10</reference>) of a dwelling, and the thing itself which is set out and established, here of the place where God’s throne is established. Having attained to this, he would lay his cause (<hi type="italic">instuere causam,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.13.18">Job 13:18</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.33.5">Job 33:5</reference>) before Him, and fill his mouth with arguments to prove that he has right on his side (תּוכחות, as <reference osisRef="Ps.38.15">Psa 38:15</reference>, of the grounds of defence, or proof that he is in the right and his opponent in the wrong). In <reference osisRef="Job.23.5">Job 23:5</reference> we may translate: I would, or: I should like (to learn); in the Hebrew, as in <hi type="italic">cognoscerem</hi>, both are expressed; the substance of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.5">Job 23:5</reference></hi> makes the optative rendering more natural. He would like to know the words with which He would meet him,<note placement="foot">אדעה is generally accented with <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, מלים with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, according to which Dachselt interprets: <hi type="italic">scirem, quae eloquia responderet mihi Deus,</hi> but this is incorrect. The old editions have correctly אדעה <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, מלים <hi type="italic">Munach</hi> (taking the place of <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi>, because the <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>-word which follows has not two syllables before the tone-syllable; vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter,</hi> ii. 104, §4).</note> and would give heed to what He would say to him. But will He condescend? will He have anything to do with the matter? -
entries.2b2fdb6a4db028bdd70d129d37cd4571608e044a: <reference osisRef="Job.23.6-Job.9.6">Job 23:6-9   6</reference>  Will He contend with me with great power? <div eID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7885" type="x-p"/> No, indeed; He will only regard me!   7  Then the upright would be disputing with Him, <div eID="gen7885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7886" type="x-p"/> And I should for ever escape my judge.   8  Yet I go eastward, He is not there, <div eID="gen7886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7887" type="x-p"/> And westward, but I perceive Him not;   9  Northwards where He worketh, but I behold Him not; <div eID="gen7887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7888" type="x-p"/> He turneth aside southwards, and I see Him not. <div eID="gen7888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7889" type="x-p"/> The question which Job, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference></hi>, puts forth: will He contend with me in the greatness or fulness of His strength, i.e., (as <reference osisRef="Job.30.18">Job 30:18</reference>) with a calling forth of all His strength? he himself answers in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference></hi>, hoping that the contrary may be the case: no, indeed, He will not do that.<note placement="foot">With this interpretation, לא should certainly have <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch;</hi> its accentuation with Mercha proceeds from another interpretation, probably <hi type="italic">non ituque ponet in me</hi> (<hi type="italic">manum suam</hi>), according to which the Targ. translates. Others, following this accentuation, take לא in the sense of הלא (vid., in Dachselt), or are at pains to obtain some other meaning from it.</note> לא is here followed not by the כּי, which is otherwise customary after a negation in the signification <hi type="italic">imo</hi>, but by the restrictive exceptive אך, which never signifies <hi type="italic">sed</hi>, sometimes <hi type="italic">verum tamen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.16">Psa 49:16</reference>; comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>), but here, as frequently, <hi type="italic">tantummodo</hi>, and, according to the hyperbaton which has been mentioned so often, is placed at the beginning of the sentence, and belongs not to the member of the sentence immediately following it, but to the whole sentence (as in Arabic also the restrictive force of the Arab. <hi type="italic">innamâ</hi> never falls upon what immediately follows it): He will do nothing but regard me (ישׂים, <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. לב, elsewhere with על of the object of regard or reflection, <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.15">Job 37:15</reference>; Jdg 19:30, and without an ellipsis, ch. <reference osisRef="Job.1.8">Job 1:8</reference>; also with אל, <reference osisRef="Job.2.3">Job 2:3</reference>, or ל, <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.20">1Sa 9:20</reference>; here designedly with בּ, which unites in itself the significations of the Arab. <hi type="italic">b</hi> and <hi type="italic">fı̂</hi>, of seizing, and of plunging into anything). Many expositors (Hirz., Ew., and others) understand <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference></hi> as expressing a wish: “Shall He contend with me with overwhelming power? No, I do not desire that; only that He may be a judge attentive to the cause, not a ruler manifesting His almighty power.” But <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference></hi>, taken thus, would be purely rhetorical, since this question (shall He, etc.) certainly cannot be seriously propounded by Job; accordingly, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job 23:6</reference></hi> is not intended as expressing a wish, but a hope. Job certainly wishes the same thing in <reference osisRef="Job.9.34">Job 9:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.21">Job 13:21</reference>; but in the course of the discussion he has gradually acquired new confidence in God, which here once more breaks through. He knows that God, if He would but be found, would also condescend to hear his defence of himself, that He would allow him to speak, and not overwhelm him with His majesty.
entries.16101c56fad704720f6dc8658ce99b7424be15bd: <reference osisRef="Job.23.10-Job.13.10">Job 23:10-13 10</reference>  For He knoweth the way that is with me: <div eID="gen7891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7892" type="x-p"/> If He should prove me, I should come forth as gold. 11  My foot held firm to His steps; <div eID="gen7892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7893" type="x-p"/> His way I kept, and turned not aside. 12  The command of His lips - I departed not from it; <div eID="gen7893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7894" type="x-p"/> More than my own determination I kept the words of His mouth. 13  Yet He remaineth by one thing, and who can turn Him? <div eID="gen7894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> And He accomplisheth what His soul desireth. <div eID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7896" type="x-p"/> That which is not merely outwardly, but inwardly with (אם) any one, is that which he thinks and knows (his consciousness), <reference osisRef="Job.9.35">Job 9:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.15.9">Job 15:9</reference>, or his willing and acting, <reference osisRef="Job.10.13">Job 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.11">Job 27:11</reference> : he is conscious of it, he intends to do it; here, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job 23:10</reference>, עם is intended in the former sense, in <reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference> in the latter. The “way with me” is that which his conscience (συνείδησις) approves (συμμαρτυρεῖ); comp. <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 134. This is known to God, so that he who is now set down as a criminal would come forth as tried gold, in the event of God allowing him to appear before Him, and subjecting him to judicial trial. בּחנני is the <hi type="italic">praet. hypotheticum</hi> so often mentioned, which is based upon the paratactic character of the Hebrew style, as <reference osisRef="Gen.44.22">Gen 44:22</reference>; Rth 2:9; Zec 13:6; Ges. §155, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. His foot has held firmly<note placement="foot">On אחז, Carey correctly observes, and it explains the form of the expression: The oriental foot has a power of grasp and tenacity, because not shackled with shoes from early childhood, of which we can form but little idea.</note> to the steps of God (אשׁוּר, together with אשּׁוּר, <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job 31:7</reference>, from אשׁר <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, to go on), so that he was always close behind Him as his predecessor (אחז( ro synon. תּמך, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.5">Pro 5:5</reference>). He guarded, i.e., observed His way, and turned not aside (אט <hi type="italic">fut. apoc. Hiph.</hi> in the intransitive sense of <hi type="italic">deflectere</hi>, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.125.5">Psa 125:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7897" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference></hi>, מצות שׂפתיו precedes as <hi type="italic">cas. absolutus</hi> (as respects the command of His lips); and what is said in this respect follows with <hi type="italic">Waw apod.</hi> (= Arab. <hi type="italic">f</hi>) without the retrospective pronoun ממּנּה (which is omitted for poetic brevity). On this prominence of a separate notion after the manner of an antecedent. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. המישׁ, like הטּה, <reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>, and הלּיז, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.21">Pro 4:21</reference>, is not causative, but simply active in signification. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference></hi> the question arises, whether צפן מן is one expression, as in <reference osisRef="Job.17.4">Job 17:4</reference>, in the sense of “hiding from another,” or whether מן is comparative. In the former sense Hirz. explains: I removed the divine will from the possible ascendancy of my own. But since צפן is familiar to the poet in the sense of preserving and laying by (צפוּנים( y, treasures, <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference>), it is more natural to explain, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.119.11">Psa 119:11</reference> : I kept the words (commands) of Thy mouth, i.e., esteemed them high and precious, more than <hi type="italic">my</hi> statute, i.e., more than what my own will prescribed for me.<note placement="foot">Wetzstein arranges the significations of צפן as follows: - 1. (Beduin) <hi type="italic">intr. fut.</hi> <hi type="italic">i,</hi> to contain one’s self, to keep still (hence in Hebr. to lie in wait), to be rapt in thought; conjug. II. <hi type="italic">c. acc. pers.</hi> to make any one thoughtful, irresolute. 2. (Hebr.) <hi type="italic">trans. fut. o,</hi> to keep anything to one’s self, to hold back, to keep to one’s self; <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. to be held back, i.e., either concealed or reserved for future use. Thus we see how, on the one hand, צפן is related to טמן, e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.20.26">Job 20:26</reference> (Arab. <hi type="italic">itmaanna</hi>, to be still); and, on the other, can interchange with צפה in the signification <hi type="italic">designare</hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.15.22">Job 15:22</reference> with <reference osisRef="Job.15.20">Job 15:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.19">Job 21:19</reference>), and to spy, lie in wait (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Psa 10:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.7">Psa 56:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.11">Pro 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.1.18">Pro 1:18</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Ps.37.32">Psa 37:32</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen7897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7898" type="x-p"/> The meaning is substantially the same; the lxx, which translates ἐν δὲ κόλπῳ μου (בּחקי), which Olsh. considers to be “perhaps correct,” destroys the significance of the confession. Hirz. rightly refers to the “law in the members,” <reference osisRef="Rom.7.23">Rom 7:23</reference> : חקּי is the expression Job uses for the law of the sinful nature which strives against the law of God, the wilful impulse of selfishness and evil passion, the law which the apostle describes as ἕτερος νόμος, in distinction from the νόμος τοῦ Θεοῦ (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 379). Job’s conscience can give him this testimony, but He, the God who so studiously avoids him, remains in one mind, viz., to treat him as a criminal; and who can turn Him from His purpose? (the same question as <reference osisRef="Job.9.12">Job 9:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.11.10">Job 11:10</reference>); His soul wills it (<hi type="italic">stat pro ratione voluntas</hi>), and He accomplishes it. Most expositors explain <hi type="italic">permanet in uno</hi> in this sense; the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is the usual ב with verbs of entering upon and persisting in anything. Others, however, take the ב as <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae:</hi> He remains one and the same, viz., in His conduct towards me (Umbr., Vaih.), or: He is one, is alone, viz., in absolute majesty (Targ. Jer.; Schult., Ew., Hlgst., Schlottm.), which is admissible, since this <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> occurs not only in the complements of a sentence (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.7">Psa 39:7</reference>, like a shadow; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa 48:10</reference>, after the manner of silver; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>, in great number; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.2">Psa 35:2</reference>, as my help), but also with the predicate of a simple sentence, be it verbal (<reference osisRef="Job.24.13">Job 24:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.3.26">Pro 3:26</reference>) or substantival (<reference osisRef="Exod.18.4">Exo 18:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.7">Psa 118:7</reference>). The same construction is found also in Arabic, where, however, it is more frequent in simple negative clauses than in affirmative (vid., <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, i. 272).
