The assertion: He is one (as in the primary monotheistic confession, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.4">Deu 6:4</reference>), is, however, an expression for the absoluteness of God, which is not suited to this connection; and if הוא באחד is intended to be understood of the unchangeable uniformity of His purpose concerning Job, the explanation: <hi type="italic">versatur (perstat) in uno,</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">hua fi wâhidin ,</hi> is not only equally, but more natural, and we therefore prefer it. <div eID="gen7898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7899" type="x-p"/> Here again God appears to Job to be his enemy. His confidence towards God is again overrun by all kinds of evil, suspicious thoughts. He seems to him to be a God of absolute caprice, who punishes where there is no ground for punishment. There is indeed a phrase of the abiding fact which he considers superior to God and himself, both being conceived of as contending parties; and this phase God avoids, He will not hear it. Into this vortex of thoughts, as terrible as they are puerile, Job is hurried forward by the persuasion that his affliction is a decree of divine justice. The friends have greatly confirmed him in this persuasion; so that his consciousness of innocence, and the idea of God as inflicting punishment, are become widely opposite extremes, between which his faith is hardly able to maintain itself. It is not his affliction in itself, but this persuasion, which precipitates him into such a depth of conflict, as the following strophe shows.
entries.bdf40454c30700e106d1ab67c7eaf3951c0e6724: <reference osisRef="Job.23.14-Job.17.14">Job 23:14-17 14</reference>  For He accomplisheth that which is appointed for me, <div eID="gen7899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7900" type="x-p"/> And much of a like kind is with Him. 15  Therefore I am troubled at His presence; <div eID="gen7900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7901" type="x-p"/> If I consider it, I am afraid of Him. 16  And God hath caused my heart to be dejected, <div eID="gen7901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> And the Almighty hath put me to confusion; 17  For I have not been destroyed before darkness, <div eID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> And before my countenance, which thick darkness covereth. <div eID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> Now it is the will of God, the absolute, which has all at once turned against him, the innocent (<reference osisRef="Job.23.13">Job 23:13</reference>); for what He has decreed against him (חקּי) He also brings to a complete fulfilment (השׁלים, as e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa 44:26</reference>); and the same troubles as those which he already suffers, God has still more abundantly decreed for him, in order to torture him gradually, but surely, to death. Job intends <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.14">Job 23:14</reference></hi> in reference to himself, not as a general assertion: it is, in general, God’s way of acting. Hahn’s objection to the other explanation, that Job’s affliction, according to his own previous assertions, has already attained its highest degree, does not refute it; for Job certainly has a term of life before him, though it be but short, in which the wondrously inventive (<reference osisRef="Job.10.16">Job 10:16</reference>) hostility of God can heap up ever new troubles for him. On the other hand, the interpretation of the expression in a general sense is opposed by the form of the expression itself, which is not that God delights to do this, but that He purposes (עמּו) to do it. It is a conclusion from the present concerning the future, such as Job is able to make with reference to himself; while he, moreover, abides by the reality in respect to the mysterious distribution of the fortunes of men. Therefore, because he is a mark for the enmity of God, without having merited it, he is confounded before His countenance, which is so angrily turned upon him (comp. פנים, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.10">Psa 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.16">Lam 4:16</reference>); if he considers it (according to the sense <hi type="italic">fut. hypothet.,</hi> as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.9">Job 23:9</reference></hi>), he trembles before Him, who recompenses faithful attachment by such torturing pain. The following connection with ל and the mention of God twice at the beginning of the affirmations, is intended to mean: (I tremble before Him), and He it is who has made me faint-hearted (הרך <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. from the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.20.3">Deu 20:3</reference>, and freq., to be tender, soft, disconcerted), and has troubled me; which is then supported in Job 23:17. <div eID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7905" type="x-p"/> His suffering which draws him on to ruin he perceives, but it is not the proper ground of his inward destruction; it is not the encircling darkness of affliction, not the mysterious form of his suffering which disconcerts him, but God’s hostile conduct towards him, His angry countenance as he seems to see it, and which he is nevertheless unable to explain. Thus also Ew., Hirz., Vaih., Hlgst., and Schlottm. explain the passage. The only other explanation worthy of mention is that which finds in <reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference> the thought already expressed in <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference> : For I was not then destroyed, in order that I might experience such mysterious suffering; and interpretation with which most of the old expositors were satisfied, and which has been revived by Rosenm., Stick., and Hahn. We translate: for I have not been destroyed before darkness (in order to be taken away from it before it came upon me), and He has not hidden darkness before my face; or as an exclamation: that I have not been destroyed! which is to be equivalent to: Had I but been ... ! Apart from this rendering of the <hi type="italic">quod non </hi>= <hi type="italic">utinam</hi>, which cannot be supported, (1) It is doubly hazardous thus to carry the לא forward to the second line in connection with verbs of different persons. (2) The darkness in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference></hi> appears (at least according to the usual interpret. <hi type="italic">caliginem</hi>) as that which is being covered, whereas it is naturally that which covers something else; wherefore Blumenfeld explains: and darkness has not hidden, viz., such pain as I must now endure, from my face. (3) The whole thought which is thus gained is without point, and meaningless, in this connection. On the other hand, the antithesis between מפּניו and מפּני, ממּנוּ and מפּני־חשׁך, is at once obvious; and this antithesis, which forces itself upon the attention, also furnishes the thought which might be expected from the context. It is unnecessary to take נצמת in a different signification from <reference osisRef="Job.6.17">Job 6:17</reference>; in Arabic <hi type="italic">ṣmt</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">conticescere;</hi> the idea of the root, however, is in general a constraining depriving of free movement. חשׁך is intended as in the question of Eliphaz, <reference osisRef="Job.22.11">Job 22:11</reference> : “Or seest thou not the darkness?” to which it perhaps refers. It is impossible, with Schlottm., to translate <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference></hi>: and before that darkness covers my face; מן is never other than a <hi type="italic">praep.,</hi> not a conjunction with power over a whole clause. It must be translated: <hi type="italic">et a facie mea quam obtegit caligo.</hi> As the absolute פנים, <reference osisRef="Job.9.27">Job 9:27</reference>, signifies the appearance of the countenance under pain, so here by it Job means his countenance distorted by pain, his deformed appearance, which, as the attributive clause affirms, is thoroughly darkened by suffering (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.30.30">Job 30:30</reference>). But it is not this darkness which stares him in the face, and threatens to swallow him up (comp. מפני־חשׁך, <reference osisRef="Job.17.12">Job 17:12</reference>); not this his miserable form, which the extremest darkness covers (on אפל, vid., <reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job 10:22</reference>), that destroys his inmost nature; but the thought that God stands forth in hostility against him, which makes his affliction so terrific, and doubly so in connection with the inalienable consciousness of his innocence. From the incomprehensible punishment which, without reason, is passing over him, he now again comes to speak of the incomprehensible connivance of God, which permits the godlessness of the world to go on unpunished.  <chapter eID="Job.23"/> <div eID="gen7905" type="x-p"/>

Actively, the steps or ways in which God himself walks, the paths of Holiness, Justice, Mercy, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> wherein he <ns0:hi>walked with,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>after God,</ns0:hi> as the Phrase is, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 5. 24. 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 23. 3. following his Example. Or 2. Passively, the steps or paths which God hath appointed men to walk in, as <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 21. 14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Neither have I gone back <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Not turned aside to any crooked or sinful path or course of Life, human Infirmity excepted. Heb. <ns0:hi>I have hid,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>laid</ns0:hi> it <ns0:hi>up,</ns0:hi> as men do their best Treasures, or what they most love and value. The Phrase notes an high estimation of it, an hearty af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fection to it, and a diligent care to preserve it.</ns0:note> from the Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandment of his Lips, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>I have hid,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>laid up.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> I have esteemed <ns0:hi>i</ns0:hi> the word of his Mouth more than <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> my ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed portion.</ns0:note> my necessary <ns0:hi>food</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>my appointed</ns0:hi> food, or <ns0:hi>my dayly portion, i. e.</ns0:hi> that food or provision which is neces<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sary for the support of my Life, as this word is used, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 22. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 30. 8. & 31. 15. which is more prized and desired than all the riches in the world.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. But he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in one <ns0:hi>mind</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Notwithstanding all these Evidences of my sincere Piety, and all my Prayers to him, he still continues in the same mind and course of afflicting me. Or, <ns0:hi>But he is, i. e.</ns0:hi> if he be, <ns0:hi>against one,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>against any man,</ns0:hi> as that word is oft used, as he now setteth himself against me. Or, <ns0:hi>But he is one,</ns0:hi> the Hebrew prefix <ns0:hi>Beth,</ns0:hi> being here the note of a Nominative Case, as it is <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 18. 8. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 68. 5. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 13. 9. and elsewhere. So the sense is, But why do I waste words to no purpose? All my former constant Integrity, and my present profession of it gives me no ease<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he is still one and the same, con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stant, unchangeable in his purposes and counsels of proceeding a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst me. Or, he is alone, and there is none besides him, who can either restrain, or advise, or move him.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 12. 13. & 12. 14.</ns0:note> who can turn him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">No man can change his Counsels or course, or encline him to shew favour to me. He is most absolute and free to do what he pleaseth, and he dealeth with me accordingly, and not by those milder Methods which he useth towards other men.</ns0:note>? and <ns0:hi>what</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 115. 3.</ns0:note> his Soul desireth even <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> he doth <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">He will not do what I please or desire, but only what pleaseth himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. For he performeth <ns0:hi>the thing that is</ns0:hi> appointed for me <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>he will perfect,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>finish my appointed portion, i. e.</ns0:hi> those calami<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties which he hath allotted to me for my portion, which as he hath begun to lay on me, so he is resolved to make a full end of them.</ns0:note>: and many such things <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">There are many such examples of Gods proceeding with men in way of absolute Soveraignty and Severity, and his Counsels and Providences, though always just, yet are oft secret, and we can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not discern the reasonableness or equity of them, which is my case.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Therefore <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">In consideration of his glorious Majesty, and soveraign, and irresistible power, by which he can do whatsoever pleaseth him, without giving any account of his matters.</ns0:note> am I troubled at his presence <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">When I present him to my thoughts. Or, when he appears or manifesteth him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self to me. Or, <ns0:hi>for fear</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>dread of him;</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>by reason of him.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>: when I consider I am afraid of him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16. For God maketh my heart soft <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>tender.</ns0:hi> He hath bruised, and broken, or melted it, so that I have no Spirit, nor Courage, nor Strength in me, as this o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the like Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 20<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 3. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 39. 11. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 7. 4. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 51. 46.</ns0:note> and the Al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mighty troubleth me:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. Because I was not cut off <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Because God did not cut me off by death.</ns0:note> before the darkness <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Before these dark and dismal miseries came upon me.
